column3: Directly completes the focus: God has encompassed and counted every person individually.
Warns disbelievers of their promised day, supporting the assured future judgment behind the command not to hurry them.
Explicitly addresses demands to hasten punishment and affirms that God's promise and timing do not fail.
Its prohibition on hastening revelation concerns a different kind of haste, though it likewise submits timing to God.
The immediate passage begins the false reliance whose adherents are then left to their counted term.
Its self-deceptive claim of only counted days contrasts with the focus's divine, exact counting of the disbelievers' span.
Describes worldly punishment and death in disbelief, but does not develop the counted delay.
Immediately precedes the focus: devils incite the disbelievers, yet their end is not to be hastened.
Those who demanded punishment receive it as the painful wind they had sought to hasten.
Names human haste and directly commands people not to hasten God's signs.
Contrasts the near and the hereafter but does not specifically concern the deferred punishment of disbelievers.
Challenges the criminals' demand to hasten a punishment that may arrive by night or day.
Uses haste and counted days in a ritual timetable, not in the judgmental sense of the focus.
The immediate continuation shows the supposed gods turning against their worshippers, extending the passage's warning.
Explains that if God hastened evil as people hasten good, their appointed term would be ended.
Declares punishment prepared for hypocrites and polytheists, though it does not address its timing.
Questions Moses's haste away from his people, a different narrative and purpose from the focus.
Directly rebukes the demand to hasten God's punishment.
Warns that God will return against persistent opponents, but the counting language is not the focus's counted term.
The same immediate sequence depicts every person coming to God alone, the outcome of the prior enumeration.
Repeats the direct rebuke of those who seek to hasten punishment.
The description of Paradise attendants has no material relation to haste, delay, or counting.
Moses's haste toward divine pleasure is distinct from the focus's instruction not to hasten punishment.
Disbelievers ask for their portion before the Day of Account, a direct form of demanding judgment early.
Legal deprivation for wrongdoing does not illuminate the focus's deferred, counted term.
The immediate passage records their words and extends their punishment, supplying the context for patient deferment.
The promised event will expose the weaker support and smaller number, linking judgment with the collapse of apparent strength.
The description of believers' faith has no substantive neighbour relation.
Its question about when the Day of Judgment is illustrates the demand for a fixed eschatological moment.
A counted monetary price has no relation to the focus's counted human term.
Fear of Satan and trust in God do not develop haste or divine enumeration.
The messenger locates knowledge with God while conveying the warning, framing the timing of the threatened event as not human-controlled.
Critiques pursuit of the immediate and its eventual punishment, a broader temporal counterpart to the focus.
The promise of no fear for the steadfast does not bear on deferred punishment.
The inability to count God's blessings only loosely contrasts with God's exact counting in the focus.
Identifies attachment to the immediate and neglect of a weighty future day, a broad temporal parallel.
The calf narrative does not develop the focus's command about the disbelievers' term.
The Day when they are tried by fire provides the outcome of the judgment-day question nearby.
Counting men among the wicked has no meaningful connection to divine counting or haste.
The sanctuary regulation and provision promise do not bear on the focus.
Directly tells wrongdoers not to hasten the allotted share of punishment like that of earlier peoples.
Counting amassed wealth concerns miserliness, not a precisely counted reprieve.
Manipulating sacred months shows temporal disobedience, but not the focus's delayed punishment.
The punishment of Lot's people is a distant example of divine judgment without a haste or counting link.
Answers those who hasten punishment by stating that Hell already encompasses the disbelievers.
God's ability to show the promised punishment supports confidence in it, though not its appointed timing.
The people demand the promised punishment, directly setting up the reply that its timing belongs to God.
Forbids rushing revelation; the shared theme of restraint is real but the setting is different.
Commands turning away and waiting for opponents, closely paralleling the focus's patient posture toward them.
The earth's extension and vegetation have no relevant relation.
The calf episode does not illuminate the counted delay of the disbelievers.
Explains that the respite granted to disbelievers is not good for them but lets their sin increase before punishment.
Questions whether continued wealth and children are good, but does not itself address the timing of judgment.
Rebukes belief after the threatened event occurs when people had previously sought to hasten it.
Affirms God's power over those promised punishment whether or not the Prophet sees it.
The forty-night appointment and calf worship do not develop the focus's warning.
The completed vengeance on earlier peoples has no material haste or counting link.
Explicitly declares God's command imminent and forbids people from seeking to hasten it.
Promises divine vengeance if the Prophet is taken away, supporting the certainty of the opponents' eventual reckoning.
The innumerability of blessings is unrelated to the finite count in the focus.
Commands leaving them until they meet their promised day, closely matching the focus's non-hastening instruction.
Directly questions why people seek evil before good and redirects them toward repentance.
Describes a brief enjoyment followed by severe punishment, clarifying the character of a delayed term.
Says that part of what they seek to hasten may already be close behind them.
Commands leaving them in diversion until they meet their promised day, a close parallel to the focus.
The retrospective counting of earthly years is a different use of counting, with only a broad temporal resonance.
Warns disbelievers that they cannot escape, reinforcing why apparent delay is not escape.
Identifies the Fire as the very ordeal they had demanded to hasten.
The denial of earthly corruption has no substantive relation to the focus.
Contrasts divine administration with human measures of time, loosely supporting the focus's divine temporal authority.
Affirms that what is promised is true, providing the certainty presupposed by patient delay.
States that the messenger does not control what they seek to hasten and that God knows the wrongdoers.
The certainty that the promised event will occur supports the focus's assurance without addressing its timing.
Directly describes people seeking evil before good while God's forgiveness and punishment remain in view.
Explains that mercy prevents immediate punishment, but a fixed appointment awaits from which there is no escape.
Love of the immediate is a broad disposition behind haste, without the focus's judgmental setting.
The enclosed Fire is an outcome of judgment but offers no link to haste or counting.
States that the punishment is delayed only because it has a named term and will come suddenly.
Promises painful punishment for persistent wrongdoers, but does not develop its deferment or count.
A numbered angelic guard tests hearers; its counting is unrelated to the focus's counted reprieve.
The forty-year wandering has a fixed duration but does not concern the focus's warning not to hasten judgment.
Human calculation of years is a distant counterpart to the divine counting in the focus.
The command not to obey deniers offers a general stance toward them, not the focus's timing rationale.
Directly characterizes humans as hasty and as calling for evil as though it were good.
Aaron's warning against calf worship has no material relation to the focus's deferred punishment.
The count of years spent on earth is a different, retrospective temporal question.
The Cain and Abel account does not illuminate haste, respite, or divine enumeration.
A benefit brought forward by God concerns promised gains, not the disbelievers' deferred punishment.
The mission of messengers as bearers of good news and warning has no specific relation here.
Moses names the calf worshipers' act as hastening God's command, a related but different narrative use of premature action.
Tells the Prophet not to grieve at their speech because God knows what they conceal and reveal, supporting patient nonreaction.
The greeting and reward of believers do not bear on the focus.
Pairs watching with patience while a people undergo a test, offering a limited procedural parallel.
The grant of mercy and high repute belongs to another section of the surah.
The regulations for prayer under threat do not illuminate the focus.
The command not to weaken in conflict does not concern delayed judgment.
Forbids concluding a marriage until its appointed term is complete, a distant legal parallel to waiting for a set time.
Counting the waiting period regulates divorce, an unrelated legal use of enumeration.
Fasting boundaries and marital permissions do not bear on the focus.
Its condemnation of associating partners does not develop haste, respite, or counted duration.
God decrees a term and holds a further specified term, providing a broad theological basis for the focus's counted span.
The decision belongs to God alone, directly limiting the human demand for the event they seek to hasten.
Every community has an appointed term that it can neither delay nor advance, directly clarifying the focus's precisely counted duration.
Hood's people demand the threatened punishment; his call to await it parallels the focus's refusal to force its arrival.
The question about when the Hour will arrive concerns the same divine control of eschatological timing.
The disbelievers ask when the promise will come, a direct demand for the timing that the focus withholds.
For every community is an appointed term that cannot be advanced or delayed, closely paralleling the counted term in the focus.
A punishment delayed until a limited term prompts mockery, directly explaining the posture answered by the focus.
Noah's opponents demand that he bring the threat he has warned them of, a close form of seeking punishment early.
Noah answers that God will bring the threatened event if He wills, preserving divine control over its arrival.
The Day is not delayed except for a numbered term, an especially close counterpart to the focus's explicit counting.
Every term has its written decree, directly grounding the focus's assurance that their span is fixed.
No community can precede its appointed term or defer it, closely paralleling the focus's measured allotment.
God postpones wrongdoers until an appointed term; once it arrives they cannot delay or advance it.
Absent a prior word and a named term, punishment would already have been inevitable, explaining why it is deferred.
The repeated challenge asking when the promise will come gives the demand for timing that the focus answers.
No community can outstrip or postpone its term, directly reinforcing the focus's counted duration.
The demand to know when the promise will arrive is a close question about the timing held back in the focus.
The question about the promised Day mirrors the pressure for a disclosed or accelerated judgment time.
God delays people to a specified term rather than punishing every wrong immediately, closely explaining the focus's restraint.
A prior word and a specified term defer the decisive judgment, directly paralleling the rationale for not hastening them.
When a person's appointed term comes, God does not defer it, reinforcing the irreversibility of fixed divine timing.
The disbelievers ask when the promise will occur, a direct counterpart to the focus's command not to hurry them.
God grants respite until a named term, offering a general but clear parallel to the counted period in the focus.
The messenger does not know whether the promised punishment is near or whether God will set a further term for it.
